title: beetle exoskeleton may facilitate body heat acting differentially across the electromagnetic spectrum
display_name: Beetle Exoskeleton May Facilitate Body Heat Acting Differentially across the Electromagnetic Spectrum
abstract: exoskeletons of beetles and their associated morphological characteristics can serve many different functions, including thermoregulation. we study the thermal role of the exoskeleton in 13 geotrupidae dung beetle species using heating experiments under controlled conditions. the main purpose was to measure the influence of heating sources (solar radiance vs. infrared), animal position (dorsal exposure vs. ventral exposure), species identity, and phylogenetic relationships on internal asymptotic temperatures and heating rates. the thermal response was significantly influenced by phylogenetic relatedness, although it was not affected by the apterous condition. the asymptotic internal temperature of specimens was not affected by the thoracic volume but was significantly higher under simulated sunlight conditions than under infrared radiation and when exposed dorsally as opposed to ventrally. there was thus a significant interaction between heating source and body position. heating rate was negatively and significantly influenced by thoracic volume, and, although insignificantly slower under simulated sunlight, it was significantly affected by body position, being faster under dorsal exposure. the results constitute the first evidence supporting the hypothesis that the beetle exoskeleton acts differentially across the electromagnetic spectrum determining internal body temperatures. this interesting finding suggests the existence of a kind of passive physiology imposed by the exoskeleton and body size, where interspecific relationships play a minor role.

title: metabolizable energy intake and sustained energy expenditure of alaskan sled dogs during heavy exertion in the cold
display_name: Metabolizable energy intake and sustained energy expenditure of Alaskan sled dogs during heavy exertion in the cold
abstract: summary objective to measure energy expenditures of alaskan sled dogs at rest and during racing under frigid conditions, using the doubly labeled water (dlw) technique. animals 18 fit alaskan sled dogs. procedure energy expenditure was measured in 9 dogs during a 490-km sled dog race by use of the dlw technique, whereby dogs were administered water enriched with nonradioactive isotopes of hydrogen and oxygen. energy intake was determined by dietary analysis. changes in background abundance of the isotopes 2 h and 18 o were monitored in 5 dogs that did not receive isotope-enriched water. results dogs completed the 490-km race at an average speed of 7 km/h at ambient temperature of 35 to 10 c. total energy expenditure, measured by the dlw technique, was 47,100 5,900 kj/d (4,400 400 kj kg -0.75 /d), and metabolizable energy intake was 44,600 kj/d (4,100 kj kg -0.75 /d) during the 70-hour race. conclusions the sustained metabolic rate for these sled dogs during racing was extraordinarily high for a large mammal. this study validated use of the dlw technique in dogs with exceptionally high energy expenditure associated with prolonged exercise in the cold. ( am j vet res 1997;58:1457 1462)

title: macrophysiology: large scale patterns in physiological traits and their ecological implications
display_name: Macrophysiology: large‐scale patterns in physiological traits and their ecological implications
abstract: a little more than a decade ago, physiological ecology lay at a cross-roads. in relatively short succession, two major symposia were convened to examine both the successes of the field and its future prospects (feder et al. 1987; calow & grace 1991). although practitioners agreed that the approaches adopted by physiological ecology had led to major advances, and in many cases could continue to do so (e.g. bartholomew 1987; bennett 1987a; woodward & diament 1991), they also argued that the field's survival would necessitate a change in approach (bennett 1987a; feder 1987a; feder & block 1991). so convincing were the warnings about the likelihood of a bleak future if the field did not alter, that among the many suggestions made for potentially productive research directions (e.g. bennett 1987b; feder 1987a; randall 1987; griffiths 1991; lawton 1991; wieser 1991) the large majority have since come to enjoy prominence. undoubtedly, some of the changes in direction have been a consequence of the development of new molecular tools (flannagan et al. 1998; feder & hofmann 1999; yocum 2001; lerman et al. 2003), and the increasing availability of sequences for entire genomes (levine & tjian 2003). however, much of the renewed vigour in the field of physiological ecology can be attributed to the enthusiasm with which the issues raised by these seminal symposia have subsequently been pursued, and to a better appreciation of scale as a key issue. of the productive research directions identified at those meetings, four stand out as having subsequently enjoyed substantial attention. these are: variation in physiological traits across all hierarchical levels (bennett 1987b; feder 1987a,b; watt 1991), comparative phylogenetic studies of physiological adaptation (huey 1987), the integration of small-scale mechanistic and large-scale ecosystem studies (grace 1991; mooney 1991), and the implications of the scaling of metabolic rates (lawton 1991; see also nagy 1987). much of the work on physiological trait variation, and the relationship between this variation and fitness, has come to be called evolutionary physiology (garland & carter 1994): the evolutionary mechanisms underlying the diversification of physiological traits and the discrete historical patterns of physiological evolution (feder, bennett & huey 2000). evolutionary physiology encompasses a wide range of approaches. these include laboratory natural or artificial selection (hoffmann & parsons 1988, 1989; graves et al. 1992; gibbs 1999), comparative studies (garland, harvey & ives 1992; grime et al. 1997; van damme & vanhooydonck 2001), molecular physiology (flannagan et al. 1998; rinehart, yocum & denlinger 2000), genetic engineering (feder, blair & figueras 1997; feder 1999), studies of physiological flexibility (hoffmann & watson 1993; huey & berrigan 1996) and mensurate investigations of the conditions necessary for natural selection (hayes, garland & dohm 1992; chappell, zuk & johnsen 1996; dohm 2002) and consequently for physiological adaptation (endler 1986; bech, langseth & gabrielsen 1999). however, it is not only in these guises that evolutionary physiology has flourished. among the several other recent developments involving investigations of physiological trait variation, three strike us as particularly noteworthy. there has been renewed and growing interest in large-scale physiological patterns. this has been precipitated partly by an increasing interest in large-scale ecological patterns and processes, or macroecology (brown & maurer 1989; brown 1995; gaston & blackburn 2000), and the physiological assumptions used to explain them (geist 1987; cushman, lawton & manly 1993; chown & gaston 1999; gaston & chown 1999; royer, osborne & beerling 2003). however, it has also become clear that analyses of large-scale physiological patterns provide a powerful way to understand the causes of physiological variation (clarke & johnston 1999; chown, addo-bediako & gaston 2002), its broader evolutionary significance (lovegrove 2000, 2001), and its implications given the prospects of substantial environmental change (hoffmann et al. 2003; sinclair, addo-bediako & chown 2003a). there is a growing realization that if research on interactions between biodiversity variation and ecosystem functioning is to develop into a broad-scale predictive science, then a fundamental understanding of the relationship between taxonomic diversity and functional diversity is required for plants, animals and microbes (hooper et al. 2002; prosser 2002; naeem & wright 2003). consequently, there is much interest in how physiological (and other) trait variation is partitioned, although to date this has been far better developed for plants than for animals (naeem, loreau & inchausti 2002). perhaps inevitably, comparable studies on microbes have been targeted at local questions, i.e. within or among neighbouring sites (e.g. nicol, glover & prosser 2003), rather than at revealing or explaining global patterns. nevertheless, the potential exists to use molecular tools, usually more readily available for prokaryotes than eukaryotes, to answer questions about diversity and function from microbial perspectives, including that of palaeoecology (canfield 1999). finally, the scaling of physiological attributes such as metabolic rate and photosynthesis with body mass, and the implications of such scaling for biodiversity at global scales have enjoyed renewed interest (currie & fritz 1993; west, brown & enquist 1997; allen, brown & gillooly 2002; koz owski & gawelczyk 2002). while these issues have by no means been settled, as is illustrated by the forum section of this issue of functional ecology, it is clear that patterns in physiological variation have profound consequences for understanding global variations in species richness and abundance. these three approaches are common to plants, animals and microbes. a fourth, and very relevant, development is confined principally to plants. this is the measurement of plant (and, to some extent, soil microbial) physiology over relatively large spatial and long temporal scales using micrometeorological, remote sensing and similar techniques (grace et al. 1995; running et al. 2000; buchmann, brookes & ehleringer 2002; baldocchi 2003; santos et al. 2003), and large-scale environmental manipulations (karnosky et al. 2003). this, by any definition, constitutes large-scale ecology, overcoming many of the problems that hampered earlier attempts to relate physiological information to landscape or global scales. however, these approaches subsume into integrated measures of ecosystem function much of the biological variation that is the focus of this article. as such, large-scale ecology , as distinct from macroecology , falls beyond our scope, but it nevertheless represents a significant and increasingly important facet of contemporary ecological and physiological research over large scales. these research areas with which we are principally concerned all have a common thread: an explicit focus on large-scale physiological variation and its implications. this approach can therefore be considered a component of evolutionary physiology: one that is distinguished by the fundamentally large-scale, or macrophysiological, perspective it embodies. for example, in the field of biological stoichiometry, studies such as those undertaken by fagan et al. (2002) and woods et al. (2003), which adopt a global scale, multitaxon approach to understanding the causes and consequences of biological variation in c, n and p contents, are clearly macrophysiological. likewise, the identification of convergent groupings of physiological and morphological traits among diverse plant species representative of different terrestrial biomes (reich et al. 1997) was possible only by taking a macrophysiological approach. here, we offer our definition of macrophysiology, highlight its connections to other aspects of ecology and physiology, and discuss three major research approaches that have had key roles to play in its development. we define macrophysiology as the investigation of variation in physiological traits over large geographical and temporal scales and the ecological implications of this variation. it is certainly not a field without historical precedent, and can trace its origins to early, large-scale comparative studies such as those of scholander et al. (1953; see also scholander 1955; janzen 1967; brett 1970; grime & hunt 1975; peters 1983), and to discussions of the value of cross-taxonomic comparisons, such as those provided by rubinstein (1992), grime et al. (1997) and huey et al. (2002). nor is it independent of smaller-scale research programmes in physiology or ecology. rather, the relationship between macrophysiology and these smaller-scale approaches to physiological diversity (e.g. mangum & hochachka 1998; feder et al. 2000; see also spicer & gaston 1999) is, in many ways, similar to that between macroecology and other ecological approaches (brown 1995; gaston & blackburn 2000). while small- and large-scale ecological approaches clearly inform one another, and certainly cannot be separated (ricklefs 1987; ricklefs & schluter 1993), macroecology provides a large-scale perspective that is essential for understanding variation in the distribution, abundance and adaptations of plants and animals, and one that is invisible if only a small-scale approach is adopted (brown & maurer 1989; lawton 1999; gaston 2000). in a similar fashion, macrophysiology cannot be divorced from smaller-scale, mechanistic investigations that characterize much of physiology. understanding the mechanistic basis of trait expression in individuals is not part of macrophysiology, but is essential for it. rather, macrophysiology is concerned with interpopulation, interspecific and higher taxonomic variation in these traits, at broad geographical scales and temporal scales, as a means to understand the reasons for variation in physiological characteristics, its evolution, and its subsequent ecological implications. a hierarchy has emerged, at least for plants, in which, at the top (global) level, key traits such as biomass allocation and growth rate scale predictably (to within one or two orders of magnitude) with body mass (over, e.g., 10 orders of magnitude of mass; niklas & enquist 2001). at the next lowest (biome) level, traits such as photosynthetic rate and leaf longevity scale predictably with one another, largely irrespective of environment or phylogeny (reich et al. 1997). the hallmark of the patterns seen at these levels is an evolutionary convergence among traits. in contrast, trait divergences among species are emphasized at the lowest (regional, community, population) levels. even so, at these levels similar groups of traits (i.e. strategies or functional types ; grime 2001) are deemed to have coevolved in different species in response to similar local selection pressures (grime et al. 1997; westoby et al. 2003; mustard et al. 2003). it is at these lowest levels that the functional diversity among traits and species is most obvious and, some would argue, most confusing (lawton 1999). most plant ecology has traditionally been done at this level. the various levels represent different, but related, axes of selection along which species traits converge but across which they diverge. at present, there is little evidence that developments at one level are strongly influencing those at another, but we suspect and hope that this will change. obviously, it is important to know at which axis (or level) one is looking and which theory is most relevant to it. developments at any level would, however, have been impossible without: (a) large, comparative studies in the lab and field that allowed the micro -physiology of individuals to be viewed in a wider what we call macrophysiological perspective; (b) access to large databases (e.g. forest biomass inventories) that were, in some cases, assembled originally for very different purposes; and (c) theories that allow disparate data to be interpreted in terms of evolutionary, biophysical and environmental constraints. just as there are clear energetic and information-based links between individuals, populations and species (feder 1987b; brooks & wiley 1988), there are also significant associations between physiological characteristics, life-history traits, behavioural characteristics and morphological attributes, given their integration in functioning individuals (calow 1977; kingsolver & srygley 2000; grime 2001; ricklefs & wikelski 2002; huey, hertz & sinervo 2003; westoby et al. 2003). macrophysiology is neither divorced from nor equivalent to life-history theory, ecomorphology or macroecology. however, unlike these latter fields, macrophysiology is concerned more with physiological trait variation at large scales, and with its direct or indirect ecological implications, than it is with variation and its implications in these other attributes. geographical variation in physiological traits has long intrigued physiologists and ecologists (tansley 1939; scholander et al. 1953; andrewartha & birch 1954; janzen 1967; macarthur 1972; prosser 1986; larcher 1995). however, there has been a recent resurgence of interest in large-scale physiological patterns. macroecology has precipitated much of this interest by asking explicit questions about interspecific variation in physiological traits across large geographical scales. for example, the mechanistic basis of the rapoport effect (the increase in range size with latitude gaston, blackburn & spicer 1998) assumes that climates become more variable towards the poles and that species physiological tolerances broaden in this direction (stevens 1989). it also implies that tropical species should show much less physiological flexibility than those living in more temperate or polar habitats, although whether they show comparable tropics-to-tundra convergence in traits as do their botanical counterparts (reich et al. 1997) remains to be seen. studies that have tested the physiological variability or flexibility assumptions (e.g. levins 1969; brett 1970; tsuji 1988; hoffmann & watson 1993; addo-bediako, chown & gaston 2000; p rtner et al. 2000) are, by the above definition, clearly macrophysiological. two further examples of ecological questions that rely on information concerning geographical variation in physiological traits concern geographical variation in animal body size (see gaston & blackburn 2000 for review) and the limits to species ranges (brown, stevens & kaufman 1996). the mechanisms underlying animal body size variation, at either the intraspecific or interspecific levels, are firmly rooted in assumptions concerning geographical variation in physiological traits, whether these have (incorrectly) to do with thermoregulation (for discussion see geist 1987; ashton 2001), or (correctly) with either fasting endurance (cushman et al. 1993; yamahira & conover 2002), or interactions between the temperature dependence of growth and development, and resource availability (partridge & french 1996; van der have & de jong 1996; chown & gaston 1999; chown & klok 2003). likewise, while there are a variety of reasons why species range limits may occur where they do (shelford 1911; gaston 2003), physiological variation and the constraints to its evolution are of considerable significance (hoffmann et al. 2001; hoffmann et al. 2003; klok, gaston & chown 2003). the impetus for large-scale, geographical studies has also arisen because of renewed interest in the utility of this approach for understanding physiological variation. although such investigations have met with some scepticism (hodkinson 2003), they plainly provide the only means to test several important hypotheses concerning physiological variation (such as interspecific metabolic cold adaptation in teleost fish; clarke & johnston 1999), and a useful way to address many others (addo-bediako, chown & gaston 2001; lovegrove 2001). moreover, these large-scale studies have also demonstrated that broad-scale environmental variation can influence physiological traits in ways that have previously gone unrecognized. perhaps the most significant examples in this regard are the probable influence that climatic variability has on continental (and indeed hemispheric) variation in mammalian metabolic rates (lovegrove 2000), and on hemispheric variation in both insect thermal tolerances (addo-bediako et al. 2000; sinclair et al. 2003a) and insect rate temperature relationships (addo-bediako, chown & gaston 2002). small-scale investigations would simply not have detected this variation. moreover, they could not possibly have provided support, from a physiological perspective, for the growing scepticism that patterns in biodiversity and the processes underlying them are consistent across the two hemispheres (blackburn & gaston 1996; chown et al. 2002; royer et al. 2003). equally, for terrestrial plants, the striking convergence seen among leaf characters (reich et al. 1997) or in the clustering of traits in relation to (mainly) nutrient availability (grime et al. 1997) would have remained undetected without large-scale comparisons across habitats and taxa. in the past, physiological ecologists were much more interested in variation in physiological traits associated with species occupation of different habitats, than with taxonomic variation per se (for discussion see bartholomew 1987). however, following demonstrations that a significant proportion of the variance in life-history traits is partitioned at higher taxonomic levels (read & harvey 1989), and the realization that species cannot be considered independent units in comparative analyses (felsenstein 1985), considerable emphasis has been placed on understanding phylogenetic variation in physiological traits as an end in itself. much of the attention has been on the exploration of comparative methods, which explicitly incorporate the idea that species are not independent and consequently that conventional statistical analyses are likely to be biased by non-independence of traits (garland, midford & ives 1999; freckleton, harvey & pagel 2002). however, there has also been considerable interest in the taxonomic (= hierarchical) levels at which variation is partitioned (huey & bennett 1987; ackerly 1999; chown, le lagadec & scholtz 1999; spicer & gaston 1999). the significance of this work goes well beyond the additional support it provides for undertaking explicitly comparative analyses in evolutionary physiology. perhaps most noteworthy in this regard is the importance of physiological trait variance partitioning for exploring the relationship between biodiversity and ecosystem functioning (naeem et al. 2002). it is widely appreciated that a comprehensive understanding of this relationship will depend on integrating approaches that use functional effect traits (i.e. those contributing to ecosystem properties) with those based on functional response traits (those determining species responses to environmental change) (hooper et al. 2002; naeem & wright 2003). indeed, the relationship between functional diversity and taxonomic diversity depends fundamentally on the extent to which a change in the environment adds or deletes a particular species or suite of species, or perhaps is responsible for modification of the species owing to their evolutionary responses, and how, in turn, this will affect ecosystem functioning (however measured). from the perspective of physiological trait variation (these traits can belong either to effect or response groups), both of these processes imply a sound understanding of the ways in which functional diversity is partitioned. while such information is not sufficient to understand the relationships between ecosystem functioning and diversity (for discussion see naeem et al. 2002), it is a necessary first step. curiously, although phylogenetic (or taxonomic) partitioning of physiological variation has been undertaken over large geographical scales (e.g. chown et al. 2002), it is rarely done for local assemblages or communities (of more immediate relevance to considerations of ecosystem functioning), and then compared across broader scales (the equivalent of investigations of spatial concordance of rarity or rank abundance in communities see gaston 1994; tokeshi 1999). indeed, this is reflected in the uncertainty with which the relationship between taxonomic diversity and functional diversity is discussed (hooper et al. 2002). clarifying these relationships would contribute significantly to current understanding of the relationship between biodiversity and ecosystem functioning. macrophysiology has much to offer in this regard (e.g. petchey & gaston 2002). research on the scaling of physiological traits with body mass has a long pedigree, perhaps more so for animals than plants (for review see schmidt-nielsen 1984). both the values of the slope and intercept of the scaling relations, and the mechanisms giving rise to these values, have been the subject of considerable discussion (e.g. gray 1981; peters 1983; schmidt-nielsen 1984; sernetz, gell ri & hofmann 1985; heusner 1991; spaargaren 1992). recently, there has been a resurgence of interest in the significance of scaling, and especially of the allometric scaling of metabolic rate. this has largely been precipitated by a host of work undertaken by west, brown, enquist and their colleagues, which has apparently confirmed the slope of 0 75 (or simple multiples of 1/4 also known as quarter-power scaling), and sought to provide a novel explanation for the mechanisms underlying it (west et al. 1997; west, brown & enquist 1999; west, woodruff & brown 2002; west et al. 2003). these authors go as far to argue that their model provides a mechanistic basis for understanding the primary role of body size in all aspects of biology. they have claimed that quarter-power scaling is the single most pervasive theme underlying all biological diversity (west et al. 1997, p. 126), because it is applicable across plants and animals and seeks to unify fundamental aspects of form and function across all the bewildering products of natural selection. in subsequent work they have explored the implications of quarter-power scaling for biodiversity variation at global scales, suggesting that variation in the abundance and richness of species can readily be explained on the basis of the scaling and temperature dependence of metabolic rates (allen et al. 2002). like other claims for unified theories (e.g. hubbell 2001), the quarter-power scaling model has generated considerable controversy. its underlying theory and broader implications have all been (e.g. & 2001; title: preferred temperatures of podarcis vaucheri from morocco: intraspecific variation and interspecific comparisons
display_name: Preferred temperatures of Podarcis vaucheri from Morocco: intraspecific variation and interspecific comparisons

authorships.name: Miguel Á. Carretero
institutions: Centro de Investigação em Biodiversidade e Recursos Genéticos

abstract: abstract preferred body temperatures (tp) were analysed in the lacertid podarcis vaucheri, from s. iberia and n. africa which has been recently revalidated as a full species within the p. hispanica complex. adult lizards from a moroccan population were exposed to a thermal gradient and tp was measured at ten time intervals. intraspecific tp variation due to sex and reproductive condition (tp: non-pregnant females males pregnant females) and time of the day (tp: early morning > rest of the day) was detected. pregnant females tended to increase their tp after egg-laying. this dependence on the reproductive condition parallels findings in other lacertids. class-by-class comparisons between p. vaucheri and p. (hispanica) liolepis from ne iberia, analysed with the same methodology, revealed higher tp values in p. vaucheri (non-pregnant females). although further research is needed to determine the evolutionary pattern of the tp divergence in this group, these results are compatible with the thermal rigidity hypothesis reinforcing the view of p. hispanica s.l. as an artificial assemblage.

title: effects of iron deficiency on cognitive function in school going adolescent females in rural area of central india
display_name: Effects of Iron Deficiency on Cognitive Function in School Going Adolescent Females in Rural Area of Central India

authorships.name: Vitaladevuni Balasubramanyam Shivkumar
institutions: Mahatma Gandhi Institute of Medical Sciences

authorships.name: Nitin Gangane
institutions: Mahatma Gandhi Institute of Medical Sciences

abstract: iron deficiency anemia is most common nutritional deficiency disorder in india and remains a formidable health challenge. girls in the period of later school age and early adolescence are prone to develop iron deficiency. iron deficiency leads to many non-hematological disturbances which include growth and development, depressed immune function in infants; reduces physical work capacity; decreases the cognitive function in both infants and adolescents. present study was done to know the prevalence of iron deficiency in both the anemic and non anemic school going adolescent girls, to assess the effect of iron deficiency on cognitive functions in anemic iron deficient and non-anemic iron deficient school girls in a village school situated in central india. methods. a secondary school having girl students in the age group of 12-15 years studying in sixth to ninth standard was selected. serum ferritin concentration was estimated by elisa. for assessing the cognitive function mathematics score, one multi-component test for memory, attention and verbal learning and intelligent quotient scores of the students were used. results. scholastic performance, iq and scores of mental balance, attention & concentration, verbal memory and recognition were decreased in iron deficient girls, both anemic and non anemic as compared to the non iron deficient girls.

title: two-way habitat use between reefs and open ocean in adult greater amberjack: evidence from biologging data
display_name: Two-way habitat use between reefs and open ocean in adult greater amberjack: evidence from biologging data

authorships.name: Takashi Sakamoto
institutions: Tokyo University of Marine Science and Technology

abstract: we investigated the relationships between vertical movements and both oceanographic features and physiological factors in greater amberjack seriola dumerili , which is a reef-associated predator in the east china sea. s. dumerili in the coastal waters of eastern taiwan were equipped with archival tags or pop-up satellite archival tags that recorded depth and temperature, resulting in a dataset covering a total of 1331 d from 12 individuals. to classify the vertical movement patterns of s. dumerili , we performed a hierarchical cluster analysis for the depth profile. we observed multiple vertical movement patterns. around topographic features, s. dumerili showed short-step dives (averaging <35 m) during both the daytime and nighttime. in contrast, s. dumerili in offshore areas showed diel vertical movements. s. dumerili occasionally performed frequent dives to approximately 150 m throughout the day. these movements may be related to foraging behaviors associated with changes in water depth. we further analyzed the response of the peritoneal cavity temperature to variations in the ambient temperature in 7 s. dumerili with archival tags. the peritoneal cavity temperatures fluctuated according to the ambient temperature changes, indicating that the vertical movement of s. dumerili is limited by physiological constraints for the maintenance of body temperature. together, our results indicate that the vertical movement of s. dumerili may be affected by the trade-off between foraging and thermoregulation.
classification_path: Medical and Health Science > Basic Medicine > Physiology > Human Physiology

title: rumination time during the summer season and its relationships with metabolic conditions and milk production
display_name: Rumination time during the summer season and its relationships with metabolic conditions and milk production
abstract: the main objective of this experiment was to monitor the rumination pattern during the summer season in lactating dairy cows and to investigate its relationships with metabolic conditions and physiological markers of heat stress. the study was carried out in an experimental freestall barn located near piacenza, italy (45 01'n, 9 40'e; 68 m above sea level), and involved 21 italian friesian cows (11 primiparous and 10 multiparous) during the summer season. rumination time (rt) was recorded by using an automatic system and data were calculated and summarized in 2-h intervals. microclimatic conditions (temperature and relative humidity) inside the barn were recorded during the trial, and the temperature-humidity index (thi) was calculated. breathing rates and rectal temperatures were recorded following stable meteorological periods characterized by lower and higher temperatures. at the same times, blood samples were collected to assess biochemical variables related to energy, protein, and mineral metabolism, as well as markers of inflammatory conditions and enzyme activity. daily milk yield, body weight, nutritional condition, and health status were also recorded. the average rt was 501 min/d, with no significant differences between primiparous and multiparous cows. according to the microclimatic conditions and physiological markers of heat stress, the cows suffered mild to moderate heat stress during the summer. a negative relationship between daily maximum thi and rt was observed (r=-0.32), with a reduction of 2.2 min of rt for every daily maximum thi unit over the threshold of daily maximum thi of 76. most of the rumination occurred during the night (on average the nighttime rt was 63.2% of daytime and nighttime rt); moreover, the proportion of nighttime rt slightly but significantly increased as thi increased. rumination time throughout the trial was negatively related to breathing rate and positively related to milk yield. daily maximum thi was negatively correlated with plasma glucose (r=-0.52) and positively correlated with plasma -hydroxybutyric acid (r=0.26). values of plasma -hydroxybutyric acid were positively related to rt through the trial. our results indicate that hot conditions negatively affect rt and modify its daily pattern. the relationship between rt and the physiological markers used in our trial support the use of rt as a marker of heat stress.
classification_path: Medical and Health Science > Basic Medicine > Physiology > Human Physiology

title: anatomy of an endogenous antagonist: relationship between agouti-related protein and proopiomelanocortin in brain
display_name: Anatomy of an Endogenous Antagonist: Relationship between Agouti-Related Protein and Proopiomelanocortin in Brain
abstract: agouti-related protein (agrp) is a recently discovered orexigenic neuropeptide that inhibits the binding and action of alpha-melanocyte-stimulating hormone derived from proopiomelanocortin (pomc) at the melanocortin 3 receptor (mc3r) and melanocortin 4 receptor (mc4r) and has been proposed to function primarily as an endogenous melanocortin antagonist. to better understand the interplay between the agrp and melanocortin signaling systems, we compared their nerve fiber distributions with each other by immunohistochemistry and their perikarya distribution with mc3r and mc4r by double in situ hybridization. although deriving from distinct cell groups, agrp and melanocortin terminals project to identical brain areas. both agrp and melanocortin neurons selectively express the mc3r, which provides a neuroanatomical basis for a dual-input circuit with biological amplification and feedback inhibition. these studies highlight a broader complexity in pomc-mediated behavior in the brain.
classification_path: Medical and Health Science > Basic Medicine > Physiology > Human Physiology

title: northeast brazilian donkeys have little physiological responses influenced by tropical conditions
display_name: Northeast Brazilian donkeys have little physiological responses influenced by tropical conditions
abstract: ten northeast brazilian donkeys were used to evaluate the influence of meteorological variables on their physiological responses in tropical conditions. physiological data included respiratory rate (rr), heart rate (hr), rectal temperature (rt), systolic blood pressure (sbp), diastolic blood pressure (dbp), mean arterial pressure (map) and cortisol concentrations. the environment was characterized using the following meteorological variables: air temperature (at), relative humidity (rh) and wind speed (ws). the variables were organized into time. the performed statistical tests included correlations, multivariate and variance analysis. the rr variable was lower in the period between 7 pm and 10 am associated with a decreased rt in the same period. differences were not detected within each time group of the day for the hr, cortisol concentrations, sbp, dbp and map. the physiological traits of the animals in this study were not affected by the time of the day according to the principal component analysis. significant results were found in the correlation analysis between the rr physiological variable and the meteorological variables of rh ( 0.66) and ws (0.69). thermoregulation mechanisms exhibit few daily cyclical variations; therefore, the northeast brazilian donkeys have little physiological responses influenced by environmental factors in the semi-arid region.
classification_path: Medical and Health Science > Basic Medicine > Physiology > Human Physiology

title: body temperature patterns and rhythmicity in free-ranging subterranean damaraland mole-rats, fukomys damarensis
display_name: Body Temperature Patterns and Rhythmicity in Free-Ranging Subterranean Damaraland Mole-Rats, Fukomys damarensis
abstract: body temperature (t(b)) is an important physiological component that affects endotherms from the cellular to whole organism level, but measurements of t(b) in the field have been noticeably skewed towards heterothermic species and seasonal comparisons are largely lacking. thus, we investigated patterns of t(b) patterns in a homeothermic, free-ranging small mammal, the damaraland mole-rat (fukomys damarensis) during both the summer and winter. variation in t(b) was significantly greater during winter than summer, and greater among males than females. interestingly, body mass had only a small effect on variation in t(b) and there was no consistent pattern relating ambient temperature to variation in t(b). generally speaking, it appears that variation in t(b) patterns varies between seasons in much the same way as in heterothermic species, just to a lesser degree. both cosinor analysis and fast fourier transform analysis revealed substantial individual variation in t(b) rhythms, even within a single colony. some individuals had no t(b) rhythms, while others appeared to exhibit multiple rhythms. these data corroborate previous laboratory work showing multiplicity of rhythms in mole-rats and suggest the variation seen in the laboratory is a true indicator of the variation seen in the wild.

title: thermal effects on locomotion in the nocturnal gecko homonota darwini (gekkonidae)
display_name: Thermal effects on locomotion in the nocturnal gecko Homonota darwini (Gekkonidae)

authorships.name: Marianne Renner
institutions: Centre National de la Recherche Scientifique

authorships.name: Víctor Cussac
institutions: Consejo Nacional de Investigaciones Científicas y Técnicas

authorships.name: Nora R. Ibargüengoytía
institutions: Consejo Nacional de Investigaciones Científicas y Técnicas

authorships.name: Jorgelina M. Boretto
institutions: Consejo Nacional de Investigaciones Científicas y Técnicas

abstract: abstract nocturnal lizards show a complex adaptation to environmental temperature. they obtain heat from the substratum, using daytime for performing physiological functions inside thermally suitable shelters, and night-time which involves locomotion and loss of heat for capturing prey. homonota darwini, the southernmost geckonid in the world, is a small nocturnal insectivorous gecko that occurs in saxicolous habitats of patagonia, argentina. geckos were captured by hand during the day on a rocky hill near bariloche (r o negro, argentina) in spring and summer. all the geckos were active during daytime and had good limb mobility with a median body temperature of 23 c. body temperatures showed a direct dependence on the temperature of the roof of the shelter and on the air temperature. geckos were made to run on a horizontal track and running speed was measured in two experiments: long runs (1 m) and sprint runs (0.20 m) during the day (diurnal) and at night (nocturnal). speed was significantly greater in sprints than in long runs and speed increased with body temperature, reaching a maximum at a body temperature of 22 c. thus, we conclude that, although the low temperatures of patagonia impose heavy constraints on the physiological performance of homonota darwini, they have a peculiar arrangement of mechanical and biochemical abilities which allows for resource acquisition at night, using cryptic habits and short sprint runs.
classification_path: Medical and Health Science > Basic Medicine > Physiology > Human Physiology

title: influence of dietary fiber content and horn status on thermoregulatory responses of brown swiss dairy cows under thermoneutral and short-term heat stress conditions
display_name: Influence of dietary fiber content and horn status on thermoregulatory responses of Brown Swiss dairy cows under thermoneutral and short-term heat stress conditions

authorships.name: Björn Kuhla
institutions: Research Institute for Farm Animal Biology (FBN)

abstract: in the present experiment, 10 horned and 10 disbudded mid-lactating brown swiss cows were included in a crossover feeding trial with a hay or hay and concentrate diet. the effects of dietary neutral detergent fiber (ndf) content and horn status on thermoregulatory responses under thermoneutral and short-term heat stress conditions were studied, as both are considered to ease the cow's thermoregulation under an environmental heat load. cows received either ad libitum hay and alfalfa pellets (85:15, c-, ndf content: 41.0%) or restricted amounts of hay and concentrate (70:30, c+, ndf content: 34.5%). the level of restriction applied with the c+ diet was determined from pre-experimental ad libitum intakes, ensuring that both diets provided the same intake of net energy for lactation (ne l ). for data collection, cows were housed in respiration chambers for 5 d. the climatic conditions were 10 c and 60% relative humidity (rh), considered thermoneutral (tn) conditions (temperature-humidity index (thi): 52) for d 1 and 2, and 25 c and 70% rh, considered heat stress (hs) conditions (thi: 74), for d 4 and 5. on d 3, the temperature and rh were increased gradually. compared with tn, hs conditions increased the water intake, skin temperature, respiration and heart rates, and endogenous heat production. they did not affect body temperature, feed intake, or milk production. lowering dietary fiber content via concentrate supplementation lowered methane and increased carbon dioxide production. it did not mitigate physiological responses to hs. although the responses of horned and disbudded cows were generally similar, the slower respiration rates of horned cows under hs conditions indicate a possible, albeit minor, role of the horn in thermoregulation. in conclusion, future investigations on nutritional strategies must be conducted to mitigate mild heat stress.
classification_path: Medical and Health Science > Basic Medicine > Physiology > Human Physiology

title: effects of a caffeine-containing energy drink on simulated soccer performance
display_name: Effects of a Caffeine-Containing Energy Drink on Simulated Soccer Performance
abstract: a caffeine-containing energy drink in a dose equivalent to 3 mg/kg increased the ability to repeatedly sprint and the distance covered at high intensity during a simulated soccer game. in addition, the caffeinated energy drink increased jump height which may represent a meaningful improvement for headers or when players are competing for a ball.
classification_path: Medical and Health Science > Basic Medicine > Physiology > Human Physiology

title: the inhibition of neurons in the central nervous pathways for thermoregulatory cold defense induces a suspended animation state in the rat
display_name: The Inhibition of Neurons in the Central Nervous Pathways for Thermoregulatory Cold Defense Induces a Suspended Animation State in the Rat
abstract: the possibility of inducing a suspended animation state similar to natural torpor would be greatly beneficial in medical science, since it would avoid the adverse consequence of the powerful autonomic activation evoked by external cooling. previous attempts to systemically inhibit metabolism were successful in mice, but practically ineffective in nonhibernators. here we show that the selective pharmacological inhibition of key neurons in the central pathways for thermoregulatory cold defense is sufficient to induce a suspended animation state, resembling natural torpor, in a nonhibernator. in rats kept at an ambient temperature of 15 c and under continuous darkness, the prolonged inhibition (6 h) of the rostral ventromedial medulla, a key area of the central nervous pathways for thermoregulatory cold defense, by means of repeated microinjections (100 nl) of the gaba a agonist muscimol (1 m m ), induced the following: (1) a massive cutaneous vasodilation; (2) drastic drops in deep brain temperature (reaching a nadir of 22.44 0.74 c), heart rate (from 440 13 to 207 12 bpm), and electroencephalography (eeg) power; (3) a modest decrease in mean arterial pressure; and (4) a progressive shift of the eeg power spectrum toward slow frequencies. after the hypothermic bout, all animals showed a massive increase in nrem sleep delta power, similarly to that occurring in natural torpor. no behavioral abnormalities were observed in the days following the treatment. our results strengthen the potential role of the cns in the induction of hibernation/torpor, since cns-driven changes in organ physiology have been shown to be sufficient to induce and maintain a suspended animation state.
classification_path: Medical and Health Science > Basic Medicine > Physiology > Human Physiology

title: insulin signaling in the hippocampus and amygdala regulates metabolism and neurobehavior
display_name: Insulin signaling in the hippocampus and amygdala regulates metabolism and neurobehavior
abstract: significance loss of insulin receptors in the brain causes metabolic and behavioral abnormalities whereas loss of igf-1 receptors in the brain leads to a developmental defect in the brain and periphery. however, less is known about the impact of brain insulin and igf-1 receptor (ir/igf1r) loss in adult mice, especially in higher neural processing regions. here, we show that loss of ir/igf1r in the hippocampus and central amygdala of adult mice results in decrease in glutamate receptors, accompanied by glucose intolerance, anxiety-like behavior, and impaired cognition. in addition, we identify an insulin/igf-1 signaling-dependent neural circuit originating from the central amygdala, which regulates interscapular brown fat activity and thermogenesis. thus, brain insulin/igf-1 signaling is important for higher neural processing and systemic metabolism.
classification_path: Medical and Health Science > Basic Medicine > Physiology > Human Physiology
